messages.subject: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: flat discrete prior and start values
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: flat discrete prior and start values
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I need to estimate the effect of 4 experimental treatments on the size of 12 populations of aquatic snails (n = 3 populations/treatment). Snails were batch-marked and captured only twice (Lincoln-Petersen design). I started from a WinBUGS code provided as teaching material by Simon Bonner ( http://people.stat.sfu.ca/~cschwarz/Consulting/Trinity/Phase2/TrinityWorkshop/Workshop-material-Simon/ <http://people.stat.sfu.ca/%7Ecschwarz/Consulting/Trinity/Phase2/TrinityWorkshop/Workshop-material-Simon/Intro_to_Bayes/intro_to_bayes_notes.pdf>). However, I am running into multiple problems (I am new to JAGS, population modelling and mark-recapture, so I might ask silly questions...):

1). The model requires sampling recapture probability p from an unknown number U of unmarked individuals (un[i] ~ dbin(p[i],U[i]) in the model below). p and U are the parameters to be estimated (I treat p as a random parameter so that the model is hierarchical). This requires providing a flat discrete prior for U, but I can't figure out how to do that. Any help with that would be greatly appreciated! As a work around, I have used a discrete informative prior produced by dbin, so that I was still able to pursue model fitting. Then, I met problem 2:

2). I can't find proper start values (from the previous posts, I see that this is a recurrent problem with JAGS). I am wondering whether this might come from the data (two populations, #1 and #7, went extinct during the course of the experiment). Would anyone have an opinion on that?

3). Finally, in case the two previous probelms would be solved, I would like to add a covariate (treatment) effect on population size (and ideally also on p), but this is another story (only commented in model code below).

Best wishes!

Eric

## 1) Model
cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen.jags", "
model{
    ## Likelihood function
      for(i in 1:pop){    #loop through populations
        ## Marked individuals
           mk[i] ~ dbin(p[i],n[i])
        ## Unmarked individuals
            un[i] ~ dbin(p[i],U[i])
        ## Population numbers
            N[i] <- n[i] + U[i]
        ##ANOVA for effects of experimental treatments on population size
        #N[i] ~ dpois(lambda)
        #log(lambda) <- alpha[treat[i]]
      }
    ## Priors for population parameters
      for(i in 1:pop){
                ## Capture probabilities
        logit(p[i]) <- lproba[i]
            lproba[i] ~ dnorm(mu,tau)
            ## Number of unmarked fish
            U[i] ~ dbin(0.1,50)    #CANNOT FIND FLAT DISCRETE DISTRIBUTION!
      }
    ## Hyperpriors for capture probability
              mu ~ dnorm(0,.001)
              tau ~ dgamma(.01,.01)
    ## Priors for ANOVA parameters
      #for(i in 1:4){    #loop through experimental treatments
      #        alpha[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
      #}
}
")

## 2) Data list
bac <- c(1:12)                            #pop indices
treat <- c(rep(c("C","S","P","SP"), 3))                #experimental treatments
n <-c(0, 20, 19, 7, 1, 20, 0, 135, 30, 190, 14, 17)        #nb captured and marked
recapt <-  c(0, 21, 18, 8, 1, 23, 0, 150, 42, 251, 18, 28)    #nb recaptured
mk <- c(0, 20, 17, 7, 1, 20 , 0, 134, 30, 186, 14, 17)        #nb marked among recaptures
un <- (recapt - mk)                        #nb unmarked among recaptures

data <- list(mk = mk, n = n, un = un, pop = length(bac))

## 3) Initial values
inits <- function(){list(lproba = rep(1, 12), U = rep(1, 12))} #c(0,1,1,1,0,3,0,2,2,2,4,2)

## 4) Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("mu", "tau", "N")
## 5) MCMC settings
ni <- 2000
nt <- 5
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3
#model
library(jagsUI)
mod <- jags(data, inits, parameters, "Lincoln_petersen.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.adapt = 2000, parallel = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric,

If you did not capture any snails on any of the two occasions for these two populations (treatments?), there is not much that you can infer for the probability p.
Therefore, the design would not allow you to get an estimate of population size in these cases.
I believe that you would have to remove these two populations and go ahead with the estimation, and report these two as inconclusive. Of course, other options would be to try multiple capture recaptures to avoid getting into no observations.
Finally, the idea to use the treatment as covariate sounds good.

Best,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: flat discrete prior and start values
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: flat discrete prior and start values
messages.body_plain:
Eric,

I believe a flat discrete distribution for capture recapture problems is typically implemented using data augmentation and a uniform (0, 1) prior for individual existence: z[i]~dbern(psi), where psi~Uniform(0, 1), and if i indexes possible individuals.    The idea is that the number of possible individuals is set to some extremely large number M, and the encounter history fed in as data is an M x numsamples matrix (for a Bernoulli encounter model), where n animals have observed encounter histories (010, 110, etc.), and M-n rows in the matrix are all zeroes: the question is how many of all of these unobserved individuals exist.  [Also note that Link (2013) strongly warns against using the discrete uniform, instead suggesting a scale prior approximated by psi~dbeta(1/M, 1); I'm not qualified to comment one way or the other].   Royle & Dorazio (2008) describe the data augmentation process in far more detail than I ever could, so that's likely a useful reference.

It seems to me that you could set up the encounter history for each site in a M rows by 2 column matrix, with the number of individuals initially marked having a 1 in the first column, and a 1 in the second column if recaptured; novel captures on the second occasion would have matrix values of 0, 1.  Technically, this is a multi-strata problem, so you might either choose to augment each site independently, or assign individuals from one large augmentation pool to each site.  Even though you can't really reconcile which individuals initially captured were recaptured, it probably doesn't matter for a straight forward constant detection type model.  I agree with Daniel that the 2 populations with 0 detections will not be particularly useful unless you treat p as constant across sites.

Anyway, probably an easier way to go about this.

John

Regarding 0 populations, I find it weird to discard these observations because they are still valuable: extinction of a population is a quite strong effect of a treatment! I think that there should be way to account for this, but don't see how yet...

Cheers,

éric

messages.subject: Bayesian analysis for fractions of mortality
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian analysis for fractions of mortality
messages.body_plain:
We run a program to retrieve and necropsy manatee carcasses.  These necropsies are used in part to assign cause of death to each carcass.  We divide cause of death into seven categories: watercraft, water control structures, entanglement, cold stress, red tide, other, and undetermined.  As usual in such things, there are a significant number of undetermined.  One issue with ignoring those in estimating fractions of mortality is the cause of death may affect one’s ability to determine the cause of death; in other words, the undetermined carcasses may have different probabilities of death causes than the known carcasses.  We are trying to estimate the overall fractions of mortality between the known causes of death (first six), incorporating our uncertainty about the undetermined deaths.

The person who held my position two people before me, Chris Fonnesbeck, developed a fairly simple Bayesian model for estimating these fractions.  He implemented it in Python (PyMC), and I’m trying to translate it into JAGS (or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS), but having some problems.  Here is one way of describing the model (further simplified to ignore details of region, year, and age):

u(i) ~ Multinomial(U, p(i))

x(i) = u(i) + y(i)

x(i) ~ Multinomial(U+Y, pi(i))

where U is the total number of undetermined carcasses, u(i) is the number of those that died of cause i, p(i) is the probability for cause i for the undetermined carcasses, y(i) is the number known to have died of cause i, Y is the total number died of determined causes, and pi(i) is the overall probability of cause i.  pi and p are given vague Dirichlet priors (all ones).

You can probably anticipate the problem I originally had in JAGS: I’m trying to define x twice, which it doesn’t allow.  With Andy Royle's help, I figured out a way around that - I can model y(i) as the sum of x(i) and -u(i) using the dsum function.  Then it didn't like my dmulti calls (Error: Unable to find appropriate sampler), so I replaced them with individual dpois calls and used dsum to tie them together to the totals.  Now it runs, but doesn't converge.  In fact, the values for x and u never budge from their starting values.

Any suggestions for implementing this model?  Is there a way to do this in JAGS or should I learn Python or try to code my own MCMC in R?  I've attached my R/JAGS code.  I can send the link to the Python code if you're interested.

Thanks,

Jeff

messages.subject: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: follow up
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

thanks to your help (and to data augmentation) I have managed to code a running (and converging) Poisson model for the effect of 4 experimental treatments on the size of 12 freshwater snail populations in 12 separated ponds (code pasted below). I have mainly used Royle, Converse and Link 2012 (arXiv), which provide two codes for that type of experimental design. However, I still have some major issues:

1) I don't really know how to deal with the two ponds (#1 and #7) in which no snail was observed (i.e., all intially introduced snails died, which is obviously a strong indication of an experimental effect). For now I use one single 00 capture history for each of these snail-absent ponds. Increasing number of 00 observations (to 20 and 100, obs object in the code) does not affect estimates of total N (the sum of all population sizes) or capture probability p, but strongly homogenizes group membership probabilities (such that estimated pop sizes become quite similar among ponds). Also, DIC increases.

2) I have a complete lack of fit (bayesian p-value of 0, very large ratio of Eobs and Esim). I have tried the negative binomial version of the model in Royle, Converse and Link 2012 (see second code pasted below) but get all negative estimates. Before really trying to understand this silly result I would like to increase the fit of the Poisson model, but don't really see how to do it.

3) To help increasing model fit I tried to make detection probability p treatment- or population- specific but, again, did not manage to do it.

Hopefully somme of you could help me with that...

Many thanks!

éric

#### DATA
bac <- c(1:12)                            #pop indices
trait <- c(rep(c("C","S","P","SP"), 3))                #experimental treatments
n <-c(0, 20, 19, 7, 1, 20, 0, 135, 30, 190, 14, 17)        #nb captured and marked at occasion 1
recapt <-  c(0, 21, 18, 8, 1, 23, 0, 150, 42, 251, 18, 28)    #nb recaptured
mk <- c(0, 20, 17, 7, 1, 20 , 0, 134, 30, 186, 14, 17)        #nb marked among recaptures at occasion 2
un <- (recapt - mk)                        #nb unmarked among recaptures at occasion 2
tobs <- n + (un)                        #total number of observed individuals
#### BUILD AUGMENTATED DATASET
#Data alone, generate 1 line with 0s for populations in which no snail was observed (pops 1 and 7)
obs <- 100    #number of lines for populations in which no individual was observed
data <- NULL
for(i in 1:length(bac)){
    if (i == 1 | i == 7) {nb <- obs} else {nb <- n[i] + un[i]}    #total number of different individuals observed
    pop <- rep(bac[i], times = nb)
    treat <- rep(trait[i], times = nb)
    y <- if (i == 1 | i == 7) rep(0, nb) else c(rep(2, times = mk[i]), rep(1, times = nb - mk[i]))
    data <- rbind(data, data.frame(pop, treat, y))
}

#Data augmentation
M <- 2000    #final size of the augmented dataset
A <- M - dim(data)[1]    #number of added individuals to reach of total pop size of M
data <- rbind(data, data.frame(pop = rep(NA, A), treat = rep(NA, A), y = rep(0, A)))

#### POISSON MODEL SPECIFICATION
setwd("~/Documents/Limnees/Article_Loïc")
cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen_poisson.jags", "
model{
### priors and constraints
  p ~ dunif(0, 1)
  for(j in 1:tr){
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    }
  psi <- sum(lam[])/M

  for(i in 1:M){
    g[i] ~ dcat(gprobs[])
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    y[i] ~ dbin(mu[i], K)
   mu[i] <- z[i]*p
    }

### likelihood
# abundance model
  for(s in 1:S){
    gprobs[s] <- lam[s]/sum(lam[1:S])
    log(lam[s]) <- beta[treat[s]]
    #goodness of fit
    Eobs[s] <- pow(tobs[s] - sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s])    #Xobs in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
    Esim[s] <- pow(lam[s]*p - sum(lam[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(lam[])*gprobs[s])     #Xsim in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
  }
#### derived quantities
N <- sum(z[1:M])
fit <- sum(Eobs[])
fit.new <http://fit.new> <- sum(Esim[])
}
")

## 2) Data list
jags.data <- list(y = data$y, g = data$pop, tr = length(levels(as.factor(trait))), treat = as.numeric(as.factor(trait)), S = length(bac), M = M, K = 2, tobs = tobs)

## 3) Initial values
nhat <- c(0,21,20,8,1,23,0,151,42,256,18,28)    #Chapman ML estimates of pop sizes (from file Pop.number.r)
inits <- function(){list(beta = rep(runif(1, -5, 5), 4), z = rep(1,M), mu.p = runif(1, -1, 1), sd.p = runif(1, 0, 3))}

## 4) Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("lam", "p", "psi", "beta", "N", "fit", "fit.new <http://fit.new>")

## 5) MCMC settings
ni <- 2000
nt <- 5
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3

#model
library(jagsUI)
mod <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "Lincoln_petersen_poisson.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.adapt = 2000, parallel = TRUE) #DIC 4451

#### NEGATIVE-BINOMIAL MODEL SPECIFICATION
setwd("~/Documents/Limnees/Article_Loïc")
cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen_negbin.jags", "
model{
### priors and constraints
  p ~ dunif(0, 1)
  for(j in 1:tr){
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    }
  a ~ dunif(0, 1000)
  b <- 1
  psi ~ dunif(0,1)

  for(i in 1:M){
    g[i] ~ dcat(gprobs[])
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    y[i] ~ dbin(mu[i], K)
    mu[i] <- z[i]*p
    }
### likelihood
# abundance model
  for(s in 1:S){
    eta[s] ~ dgamma(a,b)
    lam[s] <- beta[treat[s]]
    alpha[s] <- eta[s]*lam[s]
    gprobs[s] <- alpha[s]/sum(alpha[1:S])
    #goodness of fit
    Eobs[s] <- pow(tobs[s] - sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s]) #Xobs in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
    Esim[s] <- pow(lam[s]*p - sum(lam[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(lam[])*gprobs[s]) #Xsim in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
  }
#### derived quantities
N <- sum(z[1:M])
fit <- sum(Eobs[])
fit.new <http://fit.new> <- sum(Esim[])
}
")

## 2) Data list
jags.data <- list(y = data$y, g = data$pop, tr = length(levels(as.factor(trait))), treat = as.numeric(as.factor(trait)), S = length(bac), M = M, K = 2, tobs = tobs)

## 3) Initial values
nhat <- c(0,21,20,8,1,23,0,151,42,256,18,28)    #Chapman ML estimates of pop sizes (from file Pop.number.r)
inits <- function(){list(beta = rep(runif(1, -5, 5), 4), z = rep(1,M), p = 0.9)}

## 4) Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("lam", "p", "psi", "beta", "N", "fit", "fit.new <http://fit.new>")

## 5) MCMC settings
ni <- 2000
nt <- 5
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3

#model
library(jagsUI)
mod <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "Lincoln_petersen_negbin.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.adapt = 2000, parallel = TRUE) #DIC 3876.799
